title: Lebesgue Measure and Integration
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Measure and Integration curriculum: sigma-algebras and Borel sets, Lebesgue outer measure and measurable sets, measurable functions, construction of the Lebesgue integral, the major convergence theorems (Monotone Convergence, Fatou, Dominated Convergence), comparison with the Riemann integral, and Lp spaces.

questions.question: A sigma-algebra Sigma on a set X is a collection of subsets satisfying:
options: X is in Sigma, Sigma is closed under complementation, and Sigma is closed under countable unions
Only X and the empty set belong to it
Sigma is closed under intersection only
questions.correct_answer: X is in Sigma, Sigma is closed under complementation, and Sigma is closed under countable unions
questions.explanation: These three axioms define a sigma-algebra, the structure on which a measure is defined.

questions.question: The Borel sigma-algebra on R is defined as:
options: The smallest sigma-algebra containing all open sets of R
The collection of all subsets of R
Only the closed intervals of R
questions.correct_answer: The smallest sigma-algebra containing all open sets of R
questions.explanation: The Borel sigma-algebra is generated from the open sets, and includes all sets obtainable from them by countable unions, intersections and complements.

questions.question: The Lebesgue outer measure of an interval (a,b) is defined to be:
questions.correct_answer: b - a
questions.explanation: The outer measure of an interval agrees with its ordinary length, matching intuition.

questions.question: Lebesgue outer measure m* is defined for an arbitrary subset A of R by:
options: The infimum of the sum of lengths of open intervals in all countable covers of A
The supremum of lengths of subsets of A
The measure of the closure of A only
The number of points in A
questions.correct_answer: The infimum of the sum of lengths of open intervals in all countable covers of A
questions.explanation: Outer measure minimizes the total length of countable interval covers, giving a way to measure arbitrary sets.

questions.question: A set E in R is Lebesgue measurable, by the Caratheodory criterion, if for every set A in R:
options: m*(A) = m*(A intersect E) + m*(A intersect the complement of E)
questions.correct_answer: m*(A) = m*(A intersect E) + m*(A intersect the complement of E)
questions.explanation: This splitting condition, required to hold for every test set A, is the Caratheodory definition of measurability.

questions.question: Every set of Lebesgue outer measure zero is:
questions.correct_answer: Lebesgue measurable
questions.explanation: Any set of outer measure zero satisfies the Caratheodory criterion automatically and is therefore measurable.

questions.question: The collection of Lebesgue measurable subsets of R forms a:
questions.correct_answer: Sigma-algebra
questions.explanation: The Lebesgue measurable sets are closed under complementation and countable unions, forming a sigma-algebra that strictly contains the Borel sets.

questions.question: Lebesgue measure is countably additive, meaning that for a countable collection of pairwise disjoint measurable sets {E_n}:
options: m(union of E_n) = sum of m(E_n)
m(union of E_n) = max of m(E_n)
m(union of E_n) is strictly less than the sum of m(E_n)
questions.correct_answer: m(union of E_n) = sum of m(E_n)
questions.explanation: Countable additivity is the central property that makes Lebesgue measure a genuine measure.

questions.question: Lebesgue measure on R is translation invariant, meaning:
options: m(E + x) = m(E) for any real number x
Lebesgue measure is not translation invariant
questions.correct_answer: m(E + x) = m(E) for any real number x
questions.explanation: Shifting a measurable set by a constant does not change its measure, a natural property expected of a notion of length.

questions.question: Every countable subset of R, such as the set of rational numbers, has Lebesgue measure:
options: Equal to the number of elements
questions.correct_answer: Zero
questions.explanation: A countable set can be covered by intervals of arbitrarily small total length, so its outer measure, and hence measure, is zero.

questions.question: Using the Axiom of Choice, one can construct subsets of R that are:
questions.correct_answer: Not Lebesgue measurable
questions.explanation: The classical Vitali set construction produces a non-measurable set using the Axiom of Choice.

questions.question: A function f: R to R is Lebesgue measurable if for every real number a:
options: The set {x : f(x) > a} is a measurable set
questions.correct_answer: The set {x : f(x) > a} is a measurable set
questions.explanation: This is the standard definition of a Lebesgue measurable function, requiring preimages of rays to be measurable.

questions.question: Every continuous function on R is:
questions.correct_answer: Lebesgue measurable
questions.explanation: Continuous functions have open preimages of open sets, and open sets are Borel, hence Lebesgue, measurable.

questions.question: A simple function is one that:
options: Takes only finitely many values, each on a measurable set
questions.correct_answer: Takes only finitely many values, each on a measurable set
questions.explanation: Simple functions are the building blocks used to construct the general Lebesgue integral.

questions.question: The Lebesgue integral of a nonnegative simple function phi equal to the sum of c_i times the indicator of E_i is defined as:
options: The sum of c_i times m(E_i)
questions.correct_answer: The sum of c_i times m(E_i)
questions.explanation: The integral of a simple function is a weighted sum of the measures of the sets on which it takes each value.

questions.question: For a general nonnegative measurable function f, the Lebesgue integral is defined as:
options: The supremum of the integrals of simple functions phi with 0 <= phi <= f
The limit of Riemann sums only
The infimum of upper simple functions above f
questions.correct_answer: The supremum of the integrals of simple functions phi with 0 <= phi <= f
questions.explanation: This approximation-from-below by simple functions is the standard construction of the Lebesgue integral for nonnegative functions.

questions.question: The Monotone Convergence Theorem states that if 0 <= f_1 <= f_2 <= ... is an increasing sequence of measurable functions converging pointwise to f, then:
options: The integral of f_n converges to the integral of f
The integral of f_n converges to 0 always
The limit function f is not integrable
The integral of f_n decreases to the integral of f
questions.correct_answer: The integral of f_n converges to the integral of f
questions.explanation: The MCT allows interchange of limit and integral for monotone increasing sequences of nonnegative measurable functions.

questions.question: Fatou's Lemma states that for a sequence of nonnegative measurable functions f_n:
options: The integral of liminf f_n is at most liminf of the integral of f_n
The integral of liminf f_n equals liminf of the integral of f_n always
The integral of liminf f_n is at least liminf of the integral of f_n
Fatou's lemma applies only to decreasing sequences
questions.correct_answer: The integral of liminf f_n is at most liminf of the integral of f_n
questions.explanation: Fatou's Lemma gives a one-directional inequality that holds without requiring monotonicity or dominance conditions.

questions.question: The Dominated Convergence Theorem allows interchange of limit and integral for a sequence f_n converging pointwise to f, provided:
options: There exists an integrable function g with |f_n| <= g for all n
questions.correct_answer: There exists an integrable function g with |f_n| <= g for all n
questions.explanation: Domination by a fixed integrable function controls the sequence uniformly, justifying the interchange of limit and integral.

questions.question: A key advantage of the Lebesgue integral over the Riemann integral is that it:
options: Allows stronger convergence theorems, such as the DCT, that need not hold for the Riemann integral
Is only defined on bounded intervals
Requires the function to be continuous
questions.correct_answer: Allows stronger convergence theorems, such as the DCT, that need not hold for the Riemann integral
questions.explanation: Riemann integration lacks convenient convergence theorems for interchanging limits and integrals, a gap the Lebesgue theory fills.

questions.question: The Dirichlet function, equal to 1 on the rationals and 0 on the irrationals, on [0,1] is:
options: Lebesgue integrable with integral 0, but not Riemann integrable
Riemann integrable but not Lebesgue integrable
Integrable with value 1 in both theories
questions.correct_answer: Lebesgue integrable with integral 0, but not Riemann integrable
questions.explanation: Since the rationals have measure zero, the Dirichlet function equals 0 almost everywhere, giving Lebesgue integral 0, while its Riemann upper and lower sums never agree.

questions.question: If a function is Riemann integrable on a closed bounded interval, then it is also:
options: Lebesgue integrable, and the two integrals agree
Lebesgue integrable but with a different value
questions.correct_answer: Lebesgue integrable, and the two integrals agree
questions.explanation: The Lebesgue integral is a genuine extension of the Riemann integral, agreeing with it whenever the Riemann integral exists.

questions.question: A property is said to hold 'almost everywhere' on a set if:
options: It holds except possibly on a set of measure zero
It holds on a set of positive measure only
questions.correct_answer: It holds except possibly on a set of measure zero
questions.explanation: Almost everywhere is the measure-theoretic way of saying a property holds up to a negligible exceptional set.

questions.question: If f equals g almost everywhere and f is Lebesgue integrable, then:
options: g is also Lebesgue integrable with the same integral
The integral of f is not equal to the integral of g in general
questions.correct_answer: g is also Lebesgue integrable with the same integral
questions.explanation: Since the Lebesgue integral ignores what happens on sets of measure zero, functions equal a.e. have identical integrals.

questions.question: The Lp space, for 1 <= p < infinity, consists of measurable functions f such that:
options: The integral of |f|^p dm is finite
The integral of f dm equals 0
questions.correct_answer: The integral of |f|^p dm is finite
questions.explanation: Lp spaces collect functions whose p-th power is Lebesgue integrable, forming the basis for a family of normed function spaces.

questions.question: The Lp norm of a function f is defined by:
options: The p-th root of the integral of |f|^p dm
questions.correct_answer: The p-th root of the integral of |f|^p dm
questions.explanation: This is the standard norm on Lp spaces, generalizing the Euclidean norm to function spaces.

questions.question: The space L-infinity consists of measurable functions that are:
options: Essentially bounded, i.e. bounded outside a set of measure zero
questions.correct_answer: Essentially bounded, i.e. bounded outside a set of measure zero
questions.explanation: L-infinity consists of functions whose essential supremum (the infimum of bounds that hold almost everywhere) is finite.

questions.question: The Riesz-Fischer theorem states that for 1 <= p < infinity, the space Lp is:
questions.correct_answer: Complete, i.e. a Banach space
questions.explanation: Completeness of Lp spaces is a major result made possible by the Lebesgue theory of integration.

questions.question: Two functions f and g in Lp are identified as the same element of the space if:
options: f(x) equals g(x) for at least one x
f and g have the same domain
f and g are both continuous
questions.correct_answer: f equals g almost everywhere
questions.explanation: Lp spaces are technically spaces of equivalence classes of functions under the relation of equality almost everywhere.

questions.question: The Cantor set, though uncountable, has Lebesgue measure:
questions.correct_answer: Zero
questions.explanation: The standard Cantor set is constructed by repeatedly removing middle thirds, and the total length removed sums to 1, leaving measure zero.

questions.question: Lebesgue measure on R assigns to any single point {x} a measure of:
questions.explanation: A single point can be covered by an interval of arbitrarily small length, so its outer measure, and hence its Lebesgue measure, is zero.

questions.question: If f: [a,b] to R is Lebesgue measurable and bounded, then f is automatically:
options: Riemann integrable but not Lebesgue integrable
questions.correct_answer: Lebesgue integrable on [a,b]
questions.explanation: A bounded measurable function on a finite-measure set is always Lebesgue integrable, since its integral is trivially finite.
